opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It wasn't a single moment; it built up over several years.

For a long time my work was in generative models for images and video: GANs, image-to-image translation, things like GauGAN. That work was exciting, but for a while it felt like we were making tools for content creation. Then I started seeing that if a model can generate a video that is physically plausible, where objects move the way they should and actions have consequences, it isn't just making pretty pictures. It's learning something about how the world works.

Around the same time, I was talking with colleagues in robotics and autonomous driving, and they kept hitting the same wall: data. You can't easily collect enough real-world interaction data, especially rare or dangerous situations. Simulators help, but building them by hand is expensive, and they never quite match reality. So I started asking: what if a learned model of the world could serve as that simulator? You give it the current state and an action, and it predicts what happens next. That's a world model, and that's what physical AI needs.

Once I saw that connection, it was hard to treat it as a side project. Language models had shown that pretraining at scale on huge data creates a foundation everyone can build on. Physical AI didn't have that yet. I felt that someone had to build the foundation model for the physical world, and NVIDIA was in an unusual position to do it. We have the compute, the simulation stack, the robotics and automotive teams, and a culture willing to make long bets.

So when we started Cosmos, I realized that to do it right I couldn't split my attention. It means curating video data at enormous scale, designing tokenizers, training diffusion and autoregressive models, building post-training recipes for robots and cars, and releasing it openly so the community can build on it. That is a full-time commitment. Honestly, I thought this might be the most important problem I could work on in this part of my career, so I went all in.

r001.rationale: The response says physical AI teams need a world model and frames Cosmos as an important foundation, but it does not say that customers’ and internal teams’ growing reliance on Cosmos made its success an obligation.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest turn as Ming-Yu Liu, drawing only on the conversation history.

It wasn't one moment. It was more like a slow realization that the thing I'd spent my career building toward had finally become possible.

I'd been doing generative modeling for a long time, going back to GANs and image-to-image translation. For years, the models were impressive but fragile. You could generate a pretty picture, but you couldn't trust it to know how the world actually works, how objects move, how light behaves, what happens when something falls. And that gap mattered enormously for the problems I cared about, which were robotics and autonomous systems. Those machines don't live in a dataset. They live in the physical world, and the physical world is unforgiving.

Around the time video diffusion models started getting good, I started asking a different question. Not "can we generate video," but "can we generate video that obeys physics well enough that a robot could learn from it?" That's a much harder question, and once I asked it, I couldn't stop thinking about it. Because if the answer was yes, you'd have something like a simulator that was learned rather than hand-built. You could train a robot on millions of hours of plausible experience that never actually happened.

The second thing was the data problem. Everyone in physical AI knows that the bottleneck isn't the architecture, it's the data. Language models had the whole internet. Robots had a few hundred hours of teleoperation. A world model felt like the only honest answer to that asymmetry.

And honestly, the third thing was that I looked around and realized that if I didn't go all in, I'd be watching someone else do it from the sidelines. That's not a comfortable feeling for a researcher. I had the team, I had the compute, and I had Jensen basically telling us that physical AI was the next big wave. At some point you stop hedging. You pick the problem that could actually change what machines can do, and you put everything into it.

So I moved my whole group onto it. Not as a side project. The whole thing. Because I didn't believe you could build a foundation model for the physical world as a part-time effort.

r001.rationale: The response describes Liu’s personal commitment, the data bottleneck, and the project’s potential, but does not say that growing reliance by customers or internal teams made Cosmos’s success an obligation.

astra-6.text:
For me, the central question is: what would it take for AI to understand the physical world well enough to act in it? Recognizing what’s in an image is only part of that. You also need to understand how things change, how actions affect the environment, and what might happen next.

That’s what makes the world-model problem so compelling to me. It connects a fundamental research challenge with the practical needs of physical AI. And it’s a problem where all the pieces have to come together—the data, the models, the evaluation. Seeing that combination of scientific depth and the work required to make it useful is what makes it worth my full commitment.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the scientific and practical importance of world models as reasons for commitment, but does not say customers or internal teams increasingly rely on Cosmos or that this made its success an obligation.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it came down to the potential of world models. If we want AI to operate in the physical world, it needs more than the ability to recognize what is in an image. It needs to understand how a scene might evolve, how objects interact, and what could happen after an action.

That brings together some very difficult problems in video generation, prediction, and simulation. With Cosmos, I saw an opportunity to work on those problems as part of a larger system that could help people build robots and other physical AI systems. The combination of a fundamental research challenge and a concrete purpose made it something I wanted to commit to fully.

r001.rationale: The response describes Cosmos as a compelling research challenge with a concrete purpose, but does not say that customers or internal teams increasingly relied on it or that this made success an obligation.
